title: A block sliding down a rough ramp

stimulus.title: A block sliding down a rough ramp
stimulus.html: A block of mass m is given a push and then slides down a straight ramp tilted at angle θ above the horizontal. The coefficient of kinetic friction between the block and the ramp is μk, and μk < tan θ. Air resistance is negligible.

drawSpec.label: A dot that stands for the block on the ramp; draw each force on it as an arrow starting on the dot

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Draw a free-body diagram of the block while it slides down the ramp. Represent each force with a distinct arrow starting on the dot, and label each force with its type and the object that exerts it.

rubric.point: Gravitational force drawn straight down, labeled (F_g, Earth on block)
Normal force drawn perpendicular to the ramp surface, away from it, labeled (F_N, ramp on block)
accept: normal force tilted at θ from vertical, pointing out of the ramp

rubric.point: Kinetic friction drawn along the ramp, pointing up the slope, labeled (f_k, ramp on block), and no extra arrows (no components, net force, velocity or "force of motion")
accept: friction up the incline opposite the sliding, with exactly three forces in all

parts.sample: Three arrows start on the dot: F_g (Earth on block) straight down; F_N (ramp on block) perpendicular to the ramp surface, tilted at θ from the vertical, away from the ramp; f_k (ramp on block) parallel to the ramp, pointing up the slope. F_g is the longest. No components, velocity or net force arrows are drawn.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Derive an expression for the size of the block's acceleration in terms of θ, μk and physical constants. Begin your derivation by writing a fundamental physics principle or an equation from the reference information, and make sure it is consistent with your free-body diagram.

rubric.point: Perpendicular to the ramp: F_N = mg cos θ (no acceleration in that direction)
Along the ramp, down positive: mg sin θ − μ_k F_N = ma (Newton's second law with a term for each force in the diagram)
accept: ΣF = ma with mg sin θ and friction μ_k mg cos θ opposite

rubric.point: a = g(sin θ − μ_k cos θ)
accept: a = g sin θ − μ_k g cos θ

parts.sample: Newton's second law, with axes along and perpendicular to the ramp. Perpendicular: F_N − mg cos θ = 0, so F_N = mg cos θ. Along the ramp, down the slope positive: mg sin θ − f_k = ma, with f_k = μ_k F_N = μ_k mg cos θ. So mg sin θ − μ_k mg cos θ = ma, and a = g(sin θ − μ_k cos θ). The mass cancels.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: At t = 0 the block is already moving down the ramp at speed v0. On the axes, sketch a graph of the block's speed against time while it slides down the ramp. On the same axes, sketch with a dashed line the speed against time if the ramp were frictionless and the block started with the same v0.

rubric.point: Solid line straight and increasing, starting at v₀ on the vertical axis
accept: a linear graph with positive slope from (0, v₀)

rubric.point: Dashed line also straight, starting at v₀
accept: both lines start at the same point

rubric.point: Dashed line steeper than the solid line
accept: the frictionless slope is larger (g sin θ vs g(sin θ − μ_k cos θ))

parts.sample: Both lines start at v₀ on the speed axis and rise in straight lines (constant acceleration). The solid line (with friction) has slope g(sin θ − μ_k cos θ); the dashed line (frictionless) has the larger slope g sin θ, so it is steeper and the two lines spread apart with time.

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: A student repeats the experiment with a block of twice the mass, made of the same material. Explain how the free-body diagram, your expression in part (b), and the graph in part (c) together show how the new block's speed-time graph compares with the original one.

rubric.point: Free-body diagram: every force doubles (F_g = mg, F_N = mg cos θ, f_k = μ_k F_N all proportional to m), so the arrows keep the same proportions
accept: all three forces scale with mass

rubric.point: Expression: a = g(sin θ − μ_k cos θ) has no m, so the acceleration is unchanged
accept: mass cancels from the derived acceleration

rubric.point: Graph: same slope, so the new speed-time line lies on top of the original solid line

parts.sample: In the free-body diagram each force is proportional to the mass: F_g = mg, F_N = mg cos θ and f_k = μ_k mg cos θ all double, so the net force doubles. The second law divides that net force by the doubled mass, which is why m cancels in a = g(sin θ − μ_k cos θ). The acceleration is the same, so the slope of the speed-time graph is the same and the new block's line coincides with the original solid line.
